title: References and loops in C++
summary: Use a const reference and a range-for loop to inspect a vector.

scenario.briefing: A robotics console summarizes sensor changes held in a vector. Count the positive changes without copying the vector.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.

hints: The vector is already passed by const reference.
Add an if that tests value > 0.

misconceptions.description: Passing large objects by value by default.
misconceptions.feedback: Use const references for read-only parameters to avoid copies.
operator[] does not check bounds. Use at() when a checked access is required.

misconceptions.testDescription: The range-for loop counts positive values.
misconceptions.feedback: count += 0 never changes the count. Increment in the positive branch.

sections.title: C++ values and decisions
sections.body: C++ declares values with a type: int count = 3; double price = 12.50; bool ready = true; and std::string name = "Ada";. References name an existing object without copying it, and const prevents writes through that name. if and switch select branches, and the condition must be convertible to bool. A range-for loop visits every element: for (const int value : values) { ... }.

sections.title: C++ source files
sections.body: C++ compiles translation units separately and links them. Headers declare interfaces; source files provide definitions.

The range-for loop counts positive values.

localVerification.description: Compile main.cpp with the C++20 standard using the C++ compiler.

steps.title: Check the semantics

statements.label: A const reference lets the function read a vector without copying it.
A range-for loop visits each element in order.
std::vector checks operator[] bounds on every access.
Passing a vector by value is always cheaper than by reference.

steps.explanation: A const reference avoids a copy while preserving read-only access. A range-for loop hides the iterator mechanics.
hints: A const reference avoids a copy.
